prime.problem: You can now write one attention head, but not yet say what it can and can't see: whether it knows word order, whether sequences in a batch leak into each other, or which single line decides if a token may peek at the future. Without that, you can't tell a GPT block from a BERT-style block or a translator's.
prime.fits: This card steps back from the head you built on the self-attention card and names its properties. It reuses the masked softmax (which picks the edges) and explains why the position table from the embeddings card was needed.
expect: attention as a directed graph of nodes
encoder vs decoder blocks (the mask line)
prime.goal: Predict, for any attention setup, which tokens can influence which outputs, and turn a decoder block into an encoder block or a cross-attention block by changing one line.

attend: Which part of the head decides the graph's edges, and which part decides the edge weights?
If attention has no idea of order, where exactly does GPT get order from, and does the mask add any of it?
Why can't sequence 0 see sequence 1 even though they sit in the same tensor and go through the same matmul?
What would go wrong in training a next-character model if you deleted the masked_fill line?
In cross-attention, which of q, k, v comes from which source, and which shape sets the number of outputs?

must: Scores are dot products of contents only → nothing in the formula mentions a position → attention treats its inputs as a set (shuffle in = shuffle out) → order must be injected by adding a position embedding to x

The mask sets which scores become −∞ → −∞ becomes weight 0 after softmax → the mask is the graph's edge list → keep the triangle and token t hears only 0…t (decoder, can generate); delete it and every token hears all (encoder, sees the answer)

The batched matmul (B,T,hs) @ (B,hs,T) multiplies each sequence's matrices separately → wei is (B,T,T), never (BT,BT) → sequences in a batch can't exchange information (and it costs B·T² scores, not (BT)²)

Queries decide who is asking, keys and values decide who is answering → take q from x but k, v from another source → cross-attention: one output per query, weights over the source's length (8 queries × 6 keys → wei (4, 8, 6))
elevated: The triangular mask is tied to slot numbers → with the mask on, shuffling the tokens does not just shuffle the output (slot 0 only ever hears itself) → the mask leaks a weak sense of order, but not enough to replace position embeddings
reference: the lab's weights already include the 1/√head_size scaling from the next card
the permutation used in the lab: [3, 0, 7, 1, 6, 2, 5, 4]

compress.prompt: From memory, draw 8 nodes and the incoming edges of node 3 for a decoder and for an encoder, then write one sentence each for the five notes: graph, sets, batch, mask, source.
checklist: each node's output is a weighted sum of the values of the nodes with edges into it, with data-dependent weights
no positions in the math, so position embeddings are needed
sequences in a batch are separate pools; the matmul is batched
decoder = triangular mask (can generate), encoder = no mask (sees everything)
self-attention takes q, k, v from one x; cross-attention takes k, v from another source

retrieve.q: Explain why shuffling the 8 input tokens of an unmasked head without position embeddings gives exactly the old outputs, shuffled.
answer: each score is q·k between two tokens' contents
each output is a weighted sum over the whole set, so it doesn't depend on where the tokens sit
moving a token moves its output row with it and changes nothing else

retrieve.q: Walk through what happens to output position 2 of sequence 0 when you change token 5 of sequence 0, in a decoder head. Then do the same for an encoder head.
answer: decoder: row 2's scores against tokens 3–7 are masked to −∞, so token 5 has weight 0 → output 2 doesn't move (the lab: positions 0–4 unchanged)
encoder: token 5's key changes every row's scores and its value is mixed into every output → output 2 changes
in both cases outputs 5–7 (decoder) or all outputs (encoder) can move

retrieve.q: You're building a model that reads a whole product review and outputs one sentiment label. Encoder or decoder block? What does each choice cost you?
answer: encoder: every token sees every other, so each token's vector uses the whole review
a decoder would throw away the right-hand context for early tokens for no reason
the encoder can't generate text one token at a time, but this task doesn't need that

retrieve.q: Why does batching 4 sequences of length 8 cost 256 attention scores rather than 1,024, and what would break if it were 1,024?
answer: batched matmul: 4 × (8 × 8) = 256 pairs
one pool of 32 tokens: 32 × 32 = 1,024 pairs
then unrelated sequences would read each other and the result would depend on which sequences were batched together

compare.q: Attention never mixes examples across the batch; BatchNorm does. Which design choice causes each behaviour, and how does each fail?
answer: BatchNorm computes a mean and variance over the batch dimension, so every example's output depends on its batch-mates
attention's matmul is batched per example, so each sequence only reads itself
BatchNorm fails at batch size 1 and needs running statistics at inference
attention can't borrow information from other examples, which is what you want

compare.q: A convolution and an attention head both mix neighbouring tokens. What is fundamentally different about which neighbours they mix and with what weights?
answer: convolution: a fixed window at fixed offsets, weights learned but the same for every input
attention: any node with an edge in (set by the mask), weights recomputed from content for every input
convolution knows position through its offsets; attention has none and needs position embeddings
attention costs grow with T² per sequence; a convolution's cost grows linearly with T

compare.q: Our model is decoder-only; the original Transformer for translation used an encoder plus a decoder with cross-attention. What does each part do there, and why doesn't our Shakespeare model need the encoder?
answer: encoder: unmasked self-attention over the source sentence
decoder: masked self-attention over the output so far, plus cross-attention with q from the decoder and k, v from the encoder
we generate text with no separate source to condition on, so there's nothing to cross-attend to

predict.q: Keep the triangular mask on, still with no position embeddings, and shuffle the 8 tokens. Is the output now the old output, shuffled?
predict.answer: No: on the lab's head, allclose(out_shuffled, out[:, perm]) is False. The mask is attached to slots, not to tokens, so a token moved into slot 0 can suddenly hear only itself (its output equals its own value vector exactly). The decoder is no longer a pure set operation, but that weak sense of order is why position embeddings are still added.

apply.task: In labs/attention-notes.py, add a position table to the encoder shuffle check: after torch.manual_seed(0), make pos = torch.randn(T, C), then compare head(x + pos, mask=False) shuffled against head(x[:, perm] + pos, mask=False). Then change the cross-attention source from 6 vectors to 10 and print the shapes.
apply.done: The shuffle check with positions prints False (it printed True without them), and cross-attention with 10 source vectors gives wei (4, 8, 10) and out still (4, 8, 16).
apply.hint: Add pos after shuffling x, not before: the positions belong to the slots, and that's the whole point.
